lesson.title: When Everything Changes at Once: An Introduction to Related Rates
lesson.summary: Related rates problems connect two or more changing quantities through a single equation, then use implicit differentiation with respect to time to figure out how fast one quantity is changing based on how fast another one is.
lesson.body:
A lot of interesting real quantities are tied together by a fixed relationship even while both of them are moving. The radius of a ripple in a pond and the area it encloses are linked by A = pi r^2 at every instant, even as the ripple expands. The height of a sliding ladder and the distance its base has moved are linked by the Pythagorean theorem at every instant, even as the ladder slides. Related rates is the technique for turning a known rate of change in one of these quantities into the unknown rate of change in the other, using nothing but the fixed equation that connects them.

The key move is one you have already practiced: implicit differentiation. Previously you differentiated equations like x^2 + y^2 = 25 with respect to x, treating y as some unspecified function of x, and got terms like 2y (dy/dx) out of the chain rule. Related rates does the same thing but with a new independent variable: time, t. Every quantity in the equation, radius, area, height, distance, is treated as a function of t, even though t never appears explicitly in the equation itself. Differentiating both sides with respect to t and applying the chain rule to each variable produces exactly the rate terms you need, things like dr/dt and dA/dt.

Those rate terms are instantaneous rates, not average rates over some interval, which is the same idea introduced when you first met the instantaneous rate of a function: dA/dt is the rate the area is changing at one exact moment, not the average change over the last five seconds. This is precisely why the strategy is to differentiate first and substitute specific numbers second. The equation A = pi r^2 has to remain true for every value of r as the ripple grows, so you differentiate it as a general statement about all values of t, and only after that do you freeze the clock at the one instant you care about and plug in numbers.

Here is a first example to see the whole process end to end. Suppose a circular ripple's radius is growing at 3 centimeters per second. How fast is the enclosed area growing at the moment the radius is 5 centimeters? Start with the relationship that holds at every instant, A = pi r^2. Differentiate both sides with respect to t: dA/dt = 2 pi r (dr/dt), where the r^2 became 2r through the power rule and the extra dr/dt appeared through the chain rule because r is itself a function of t. Now substitute the values that describe this particular instant: r = 5 and dr/dt = 3. That gives dA/dt = 2 pi (5)(3) = 30 pi square centimeters per second. Notice the units: a length rate (cm/s) turned into an area rate (cm^2/s), which is exactly the kind of unit shift you should expect whenever the governing equation involves a squared or cubed variable.

This example is small enough to set up in your head, but most related rates problems are word problems buried in a paragraph of description, involving triangles, cones, or moving vehicles. The next few sections build a reliable procedure, starting with a five-step method, for turning any such paragraph into an equation you can differentiate just like this one.
